analysis.one_liner: Sets patient protections in managed care plans, with outside appeals, faster decisions, and limited lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The Frist-Breaux-Jeffords patients' rights bill was introduced in May 2001 and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, where it died without a hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bipartisan bill, sponsored by Sen. Bill Frist with Sens. John Breaux and Jim Jeffords, would have set a national list of patient protections for people in HMOs and other managed care plans. It guaranteed access to emergency care and emergency ambulance rides under a "prudent layperson" standard, direct access to OB-GYNs and pediatricians, faster decisions on treatment requests, a fair outside appeal when a plan denies care, disclosure of plan costs and rules, and rules for continuing care with a doctor whose contract the plan dropped. It also would have created penalties for plans that fail to provide required benefits and limited certain class action lawsuits, while letting states keep stronger protections. It never received a single hearing, amendment, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: About 160 million Americans covered by employer health plans at the time, especially people in HMOs: patients needing urgent emergency care, women needing OB-GYN care, children needing pediatricians, the chronically ill needing specialists and continuity of care, cancer patients seeking clinical trials, and breast cancer patients needing adequate hospital stays. Health care providers also benefited from limits on managed-care interference with medical decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in employer-provided HMOs and managed care plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires health plans to cover emergency room care and emergency ambulance transport whenever a prudent layperson would judge them necessary, with no prior authorization needed, and bars plans from charging patients extra for out-of-network emergency care.
Lets women go directly to their OB-GYN without a referral from a primary care doctor, and lets parents pick a pediatrician as their child's primary care provider.

Requires plans to make prior authorization decisions within set deadlines (72 hours when a delay would jeopardize life or health) and creates a formal internal appeal plus an independent external medical review when a plan denies a benefit.

Creates civil monetary penalties for plans that fail to provide benefits not subject to medical review, and gives patients court remedies against plans, while limiting certain class action litigation.

Requires plans to disclose benefits, cost-sharing, exclusions, medical-necessity definitions, provider directories, and appeals procedures in plain, accessible language, with penalties for non-compliance.

Requires plans to cover routine patient costs for people with life-threatening or serious illnesses who join federally approved clinical trials, and mandates minimum inpatient stays after mastectomies and full coverage of secondary cancer consultations.

Protects the right to continued treatment for up to 90 days (longer for pregnancy and terminal illness) with a doctor whose contract the plan dropped, and bans plans from gagging doctors from discussing all treatment options with patients.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, HMOs, and self-insured employers would bear compliance, external-review, and litigation costs, some of which would be passed through to premiums, while patients would face additional care costs (partially offset by reduced cost-shifting).

drawbacks.text: The bill was a compromise that gave patients less power to sue than the Democratic-backed Norwood-Dingell bill: the right to hold plans accountable was confined to independent external review and civil penalties for limited benefits, with limits on class action litigation.

Several key protections had exemptions and cost-shifting carve-outs: point-of-service choice was not required for small employers (2-25 employees), plans could still charge higher cost-sharing for out-of-network point-of-service care, and external review and fines apply only to certain benefit determinations rather than all medical judgments.

The emergency-services protections applied only where plans offered such coverage and excluded services the plan had already excluded, and nonparticipating-provider reimbursement for post-stabilization care could end quickly once the plan arranged a transfer.

Employers argued that the threat of lawsuits and new mandates would raise premiums and prompt some employers to drop coverage, which is why liability remained the most contentious issue in the 107th Congress debate over patients' rights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients in managed care plans the benefits were real and concrete: quicker access to emergency and specialty care, an independent reviewer to overrule wrongful denials, and plain-language disclosure of what a plan would and would not pay for. The compromise design deliberately limited what patients could recover in court, which was the central objection from those who wanted fuller liability against HMOs. Insurers and employers would bear real compliance and premium costs, so the bill traded a modest cost to concentrated interests for significant protections for the insured public, but it was narrower than the strongest version of a patients' bill of rights that was debated at the time.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in May 2001, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Frist, along with Sens. John Breaux and Jim Jeffords, introduced the Bipartisan Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 2001 on May 15, 2001 as a bipartisan middle-ground alternative in the managed care debate.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, its first and last formal action.

No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no placement on the Senate calendar, and no floor consideration through the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, HMOs, and self-insured employers were better off because the bill never advanced: they avoided new patient-protection mandates, external review requirements, disclosure penalties, and expanded patient remedies. Managed care plans continued to operate under prior law without the federal protections this bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sen. Bill Frist
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 15, 2001 and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up: no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled after referral, and the Congress ended with the bill still in committee.

against.name: Insurers, HMOs, and employer groups opposing liability provisions
against.what_they_did: Opposed strong patients' rights and liability provisions in the 107th Congress, making managed care legislation politically difficult and contributing to the Senate's inability to move any version to law.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan and independent (one Republican, one Democrat, one Independent), so the outcome cannot be attributed to party-line opposition; the record simply shows inaction rather than a partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill required plans to cover emergency care without prior authorization, speed up determinations, disclose plan terms, cover clinical trial costs, and pay civil fines for failures to provide benefits, and created patient court remedies. Its main cost would fall on managed care plans, which strongly opposed the liability and review provisions.

As plan sponsors, employers would have absorbed compliance costs, faster timelines, external review expenses, and expanded patient remedies, and the business community fought to keep new litigation exposure out of ERISA plans. The bill's limits on class actions and its compromise scope were partly designed to reduce their exposure.

Providers would have gained from faster determinations, fewer restrictions on medical advice, penalties on plans for cutting care, and continuity-of-care requirements, though they also would have faced new plan rules on reimbursement, notification, and adherence to plan quality standards.
